title: Raga Maru
hook: the raga of courage, traditionally sung before battle

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Mali Gaura, and your line was sweet and short: Namdev blessing the wool.

Calm and deep. Lively. Short and sweet, with a blanket blessed. All week the ragas kept changing color. Now the mood turns. The next section of the Guru Granth Sahib is Raga Maru, and tradition says it was sung before battle, when people needed their nerve. It's a hard mood to sing about: being afraid, and going anyway.

Maru is a long section, and it holds hymns that look hard things in the face: death, loss, the shortness of a life. Tradition remembers it as a raga for the eve of battle. Its hymn is for tomorrow. Today, the color itself: courage. To hear what courage means here, go back to the Granth's first page. The Mul Mantar, the root statement, names the One with a short list. Among its words are nirbhau, without fear, which you met on day 544, and nirvair, without hate. They sit side by side. The courage the Granth honors isn't anger loud enough to drown out fear. It's fearlessness with no hatred in it. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, puts it in one line near the end of the Granth, in plain English, not word for word: the wise one frightens no one, and fears no one. Both halves count. Fearing no one but frightening everyone isn't the picture. Neither is frightening no one only because you're too scared to stand up. And Maru's hymns keep pointing past the battlefield, to the fear inside a person, of loss, of being judged, of dying, and to the Name as the ground to stand on. So the raga of battle is also a raga of steadiness. That's today's line: courage.
screen: `A RAGA FOR THE EVE OF BATTLE.` · `NIRBHAU AND NIRVAIR, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.` · `THE FEAR INSIDE, THE GROUND TO STAND ON.` · then, large: `COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Plant your feet flat on the floor, feel their weight, and let your back be tall. Bring to mind one thing you've been putting off because it scares you a little, a phone call, an honest no, and look at it from where you sit without solving it: breathe in and feel the ground, breathe out and let go of any blame attached to it. If you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath; if you don't, keep your feet planted and your breath steady.
Raga Maru. The raga tradition remembers being sung before battle, whose courage, in the Granth's terms, is without fear and without hate. Today's word.
Your line: courage. Without fear, and without making anyone else afraid. That makes a week.

howItsDone: Shabads from the Maru section are sung in Raga Maru in kirtan. Sikhs recite the Mul Mantar, with its words nirbhau and nirvair, at the start of daily prayer, and it stands at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib.

chat.says: If Maru was sung before battle, does Sikh courage mean being angry enough not to fear?
options: No. The Granth pairs without fear and without hate: fear no one, frighten no one.
Yes. Anger is the fuel that lets a warrior forget fear on the field.
No. Courage means never facing anyone, so nobody gets frightened.
